summary: A 1978 specification of JANUS, a symmetrical, 1822-like interface for the Packet Radio project to connect radio units to other equipment. It is related to BBN Report 1822 for the ARPANET.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 745 defines JANUS, an 1822-like interface intended to work the same way at both ends. It specifies electrical and low-level protocol behavior, while leaving higher-level message formats to applications.

questions: why do network interfaces need symmetry
why does janus require a four way handshake
subtitle: A symmetrical, 1822-like interface for connecting paired devices.

tldr.problem: The 1822 interface has host-specific and IMP-specific details, so two interfaces intended for different sides may not work when connected to each other.
tldr.mechanism: JANUS specifies a symmetrical interface, clarifying low-level handshaking, message padding and electrical requirements for distant connections.
tldr.outcome: The interface was designed for Packet Radio units and other equipment. Higher-level software protocols remain outside the memo's scope.

today: RFC 745 specifies the JANUS interface for the Packet Radio project and other possible applications. The memo limits its scope to the electrical interface and low-level protocol, not application-level protocols.

sections.title: Why a Symmetrical Interface
sections.content:
The Packet Radio project needed an interface between radio units and other equipment. The RFC explains that although Report 1822 describes transfer in each direction as identical, some aspects are specific to the host side or IMP side.

JANUS respecifies those aspects so that two JANUS interfaces can be interchangeable. The memo uses “home interface” and “foreign interface” in place of host and IMP.
sections.plainLanguage: Some 1822 details depended on which side was the host and which was the IMP. JANUS defines both ends alike so paired devices can connect directly.

sections.title: Low-Level Protocol Rules
sections.content:
JANUS requires received messages to be padded to a full word with zeros and requires interfaces to accept messages up to 8160 bits for ARPANET-compatible use. It requires the four-way handshake and prohibits the two-way option described in Report 1822.

The memo also specifies timing, including a delay of one-tenth of a second after raising Ready to avoid relay-contact bounce, and requires the high-order bit of each word to be transmitted first.
sections.plainLanguage: The interface rules specify how messages are padded and how the two sides coordinate each bit. JANUS requires a four-way handshake because the memo identifies failure risks with the two-way method.

sections.title: Distant-Host Electrical Requirements
sections.content:
For distant-host connections, the memo specifies signal levels and waveforms based on EIA RS-422. It requires a receiver to operate across a common-mode voltage range from -100 to +100 volts and not be permanently damaged from -300 to +300 volts.

The receiver uses optical isolation or another method not sensitive to rise and hold times. The memo also specifies cable shielding and termination requirements.
sections.plainLanguage: For distant connections, JANUS sets voltage and isolation requirements so different ground potentials are less likely to damage the receiver. It also specifies cable and shield behavior.

sections.title: Compatibility with 1822
sections.content:
The RFC says the low-level protocol requirements clarify Report 1822 and the local signal levels are compatible. The main potential difficulties are in the distant-host electrical interface.

It notes differences in cable impedance, electrical isolation, and maximum input voltage, and says attention is needed when connecting JANUS and 1822 interfaces.
sections.plainLanguage: JANUS was designed to interoperate with 1822 in many applications, but the distant-host electrical differences need attention.
